items.title: Every odd-degree real polynomial has a real root
items.strategy: For a real polynomial of odd degree with nonzero leading coefficient, choose a large positive radius so the leading term dominates the sum of the lower terms in absolute value. This forces opposite signs at a large positive and a large negative argument. The published continuity of real polynomial functions and the intermediate value theorem then give a real root.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb R$ has degree $1$ or an even degree
items.strategy: If an irreducible real polynomial had odd degree greater than one, the odd-degree theorem would give a real root. The factor theorem would then give a nontrivial linear factor over $\mathbb R$, contradicting irreducibility.

items.title: To prove the fundamental theorem of algebra, it suffices to split every real polynomial over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Assume every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$. For a nonconstant polynomial $g\in\mathbb C[x]$, write $g=u+iv$ with $u,v\in\mathbb R[x]$ and form the conjugate polynomial $\overline g=u-iv$. Then $g\overline g\in\mathbb R[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$, so it has a complex root $z$. Because $\mathbb C$ is a field, $g(z)\overline{g(z)}=0$ forces $g(z)=0$ or $\overline g(z)=0$, and the second case gives a root of $g$ after conjugating. Therefore every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ has a complex root, which is the definition of algebraic closedness.

items.title: A quadratic extension in characteristic not $2$ is obtained by adjoining a square root
items.strategy: Let $E/F$ have degree $2$ and pick $\alpha\in E\setminus F$. Its minimal polynomial over $F$ has degree $2$, so after writing it as $x^2+bx+c$ the quadratic formula expresses $\alpha$ in $F(\sqrt{b^2-4c})$. Because the extension already has degree $2$, this generated subfield is all of $E$.

items.title: A field is algebraically closed exactly when every nonconstant polynomial splits, equivalently when it has no nontrivial finite extension
items.strategy: From algebraic closedness, repeatedly apply the factor theorem to peel off linear factors and show every nonconstant polynomial splits. If every nonconstant polynomial splits, then any finite extension generated by an algebraic element must be trivial because its minimal polynomial already splits into linear factors over the base. Conversely, if the field has no nontrivial finite extension, then adjoining a root of an irreducible polynomial would create a nontrivial finite extension, so every irreducible polynomial already has a root in the field and the field is algebraically closed.

items.title: The complex numbers are algebraically closed
items.strategy: Use the reduction lemma to work with a nonconstant real polynomial $f$. Let $E$ be a splitting field of $f(x)(x^2+1)$ over $\mathbb R$. By characteristic zero, the extension $E/\mathbb R$ is finite Galois, and because $x^2+1$ splits in $E$ one has $\mathbb C\subseteq E$. Let $H$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb R)$ and let $M=E^H$. The fixed-field degree $[M:\mathbb R]=[G:H]$ is odd, so for every $\alpha\in M$ the minimal-polynomial degree $[\mathbb R(\alpha):\mathbb R]$ divides an odd number and is therefore odd; the odd-degree irreducibility corollary forces it to be $1$, hence $M=\mathbb R$ and $G$ is a $2$-group. Then $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb C)$ is a finite $2$-group. If it were nontrivial, the index-$2$ subgroup theorem would give an intermediate quadratic extension of $\mathbb C$, but the quadratic-extension lemma and the published complex square-root theorem rule those out. Therefore $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb C)=1$, so $E=\mathbb C$, $f$ splits over $\mathbb C$, and the reduction lemma finishes the proof.

items.title: Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits into linear factors
items.strategy: The main theorem says $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed. Apply the equivalence proposition to convert that root-existence statement into full splitting.

items.title: The complex numbers form an algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: Combine the main theorem with the published fact that $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a degree-$2$ extension. The definition of algebraic closure then applies immediately.

items.title: The algebraic numbers in $\mathbb C$ form an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb C$ be the subfield of elements algebraic over $\mathbb Q$. The published subfield theorem gives that $A$ is a field. For a nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in $A$, the main theorem gives a root $z\in\mathbb C$. Adjoining the finitely many algebraic coefficients and then $z$ produces a finite extension of $\mathbb Q$, so $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ and therefore lies in $A$. Thus $A$ is algebraically closed and algebraic over $\mathbb Q$, hence is an algebraic closure.

items.title: A nonreal root of a real polynomial comes with its complex conjugate
items.strategy: If $f\in\mathbb R[x]$ and $f(z)=0$, apply complex conjugation to the coefficient expression. Because conjugation fixes $\mathbb R$ pointwise and is a field automorphism of $\mathbb C$, the conjugated equation is exactly $f(\overline z)=0$.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ has degree $1$ or $2$
items.strategy: Let $f\in\mathbb R[x]$ be irreducible. By the fundamental theorem of algebra it has a complex root $z$. If $z$ is real, irreducibility forces $f$ to be linear. If $z$ is nonreal, the conjugate-pair lemma gives the quadratic polynomial $(x-z)(x-\overline z)\in\mathbb R[x]$, and the minimal polynomial of $z$ over $\mathbb R$ divides that quadratic. Since the minimal polynomial is $f$ and is not linear, its degree is $2$.

items.title: Every real polynomial factors into linear and irreducible quadratic factors
items.strategy: Factor the polynomial into irreducibles in $\mathbb R[x]$ using the published polynomial-factorization theorem. The preceding corollary says each irreducible factor has degree $1$ or $2$, and every degree-$2$ irreducible factor is already quadratic.

items.title: A complex polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity
items.strategy: Use the splitting corollary to write a degree-$n$ polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ as a product of $n$ linear factors. Group equal roots together; the exponents are their multiplicities. The UFD property of $\mathbb C[x]$ makes that multiplicity data well defined, and the total multiplicity is exactly the original degree.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb R$ and over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Show that $x^3-2$ has one real root and one irreducible quadratic factor over $\mathbb R$, then split the quadratic over $\mathbb C$ by adjoining the primitive cube roots of unity. The point is the visible difference between the real and complex factorizations of the same polynomial.

items.title: $x^4+1$ factors over $\mathbb R$ into two irreducible quadratics
items.strategy: Start from the complex fourth roots of $-1$, pair conjugates, and multiply each pair to recover the two real quadratic factors. This is the clean witness that irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ and irreducible over $\mathbb R$ are different questions.

items.title: $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb R$ and split over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Use the published irreducibility item over $\mathbb R$, and then factor $x^2+1=(x-i)(x+i)$ over $\mathbb C$. This is the smallest concrete instance of the theorem.

items.title: $x^5-x-1$ has a real root
items.strategy: Evaluate the polynomial at two explicit real numbers with opposite signs and invoke the odd-degree theorem. The example exists to make the analytic input visible on a nontrivial odd-degree polynomial.

items.title: $x^5-6x+3$ over $\mathbb Q$ is not solvable by radicals
items.strategy: Use Eisenstein at $3$ to prove irreducibility. The derivative $5x^4-6$ has exactly two real zeros, and sign checks plus the intermediate value theorem show the quintic has exactly three real roots, so its splitting field inside $\mathbb C$ has exactly one nontrivial complex-conjugation orbit on roots, giving a transposition in the Galois group. Irreducibility makes the degree-$5$ action transitive, so the published prime-degree transposition theorem gives the full group $S_5$. Since $S_5$ is not solvable, the solvable-by-radicals implication rules the polynomial out.

items.title: FALSE: every polynomial with real coefficients has a real root
items.strategy: Refute the statement with $x^2+1$, whose real irreducibility is already published and whose graph never meets the real axis.

items.title: FALSE: the real numbers are algebraically closed
items.strategy: Use the same polynomial $x^2+1$: it has no root in $\mathbb R$, so $\mathbb R$ fails the defining root-existence property of an algebraically closed field.

items.title: FALSE: every irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ has degree $1$
items.strategy: The irreducible quadratic $x^2+1$ is the smallest counterexample, and the A page explains why degree $2$ is the exact upper bound.

items.title: FALSE: every irreducible quintic over $\mathbb Q$ is insoluble by radicals
items.strategy: Refute the universal claim with the irreducible quintic $x^5-2$. Eisenstein at $2$ shows irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$, while its five roots lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_5,\sqrt[5]{2})$, so its splitting field is contained in a radical extension of $\mathbb Q$ and the polynomial is solvable by radicals. This preserves the intended contrast with the neighbouring insoluble irreducible quintic without duplicating the already-published broader false statement that not every quintic is insoluble by radicals.

items.title: The Artin and minimum-modulus proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra use different machinery
items.strategy: Write this as the design's required agreement record. It compares two proofs of the same theorem, not two pages of the library: this page's proof uses only the intermediate value theorem together with Galois theory and Sylow theory, while the later proof on `the-complex-exponential-and-eulers-formula` uses the minimum-modulus route. At authoring, give the remark `forward_refs: [thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra-minimum-modulus-proof]` and no dependency edge to that later theorem.
